newsitem.title: USA: Johnson Controls workers approve contracts.
newsitem.headline: Johnson Controls workers approve contracts.

text.p: Members of the United Auto Workers at Johson Controls Inc's truck-seat plants in Michigan and Ohio approved their first union contracts on Friday, bringing an end to a 25-day strike that disrupted Ford Motor Co truck production.
Production at Johnson's Plymouth, Mich., plant could resume as early as Friday night, while another plant in Oberlin, Ohio, will restart production later this weekend, union officials said.
The more than 300 Plymouth workers approved their new pact by an 82 percent margin, while 200 Oberlin workers approved their new contract by an 83 percent margin.
The new three-year pact will boost workers' pay 22 percent to 50 percent over the next 24 months.

For example, a seat assembler at Plymouth who made $10.50 an hour without a union contract will receive an immediate increase to $12 an hour, and will earn $14 an hour by the end of the contract -- an overall increase of 33 percent.
The negotiations between Johnson Controls and the UAW were closely watched by the auto parts industry, where the union is making a major push to organize workers.

Bob King, director of UAW Region 1A, said he would now focus his efforts on organizing workers at Johnson's Taylor, Mich., plant, which builds seats for Chrysler Corp.'s Jeep Grand Cherokee sport/utility vehicles.
"I really hope between Chrysler, JCI and UAW we can sit down and work this out intelligently," he said.
The new contracts do not require Johnson Controls to pledge neutrality in future UAW organizing drives.
Only six of Johnson's 34 plants are unionized.

The strikes at Plymouth and Oberlin forced Ford temporarily to halt production of its Expedition sport/utility vehicle in Wayne, Mich., and its Econoline van in Lorain, Ohio. In a move that shocked the supplier industry, Ford refused to accept seats made by non-union replacement workers.
Ford spokesman Bert Serre said the Lorain production line would resume operations on Monday.
Ford restarted Expedition production on February 12 by shifting rear-seat production to Johnson's rival, Lear Corp., and by producing front seats at its own Chesterfield, Mich., trim plant.

Serre said Johnson Controls would focus on building seats for regular Expedition production, while Lear and Chesterfield would assemble seats to retrofit 13,700 Expeditions that were built without seats and stored. The retrofitting will occur in an empty Brighton, Mich., plant once used to install convertible tops on Ford Mustang coupes.
Once the retrofits are complete, Johnson Controls will again become the sole producer of seats for the Expedition and Econoline, Serre said.
